What’s in a Name?

Time, Place and Recorded Sex in American First Names

Authors
Affiliation

Group AJ · HEC Lausanne

Group AJ · HEC Lausanne

Published

16 November 2026

Abstract

We examine American first names across time, states and recorded sex using Social Security Administration national data for 1880–2025 and state data for 1910–2025. The analysis addresses three questions: popularity life cycles and spelling, geographical differences, and changes in name–sex associations. Among 815 selected name–sex series, the median number of observed years near peak popularity falls from about 45 for the earliest peak decades to 17–23 for peak decades from the 1950s onward. Final-letter patterns also vary strongly across periods. State naming distributions become more similar between 1930 and 1985 under a descriptive divergence measure, although suppression and early coverage prevent a fully adjusted comparison. Among names common both historically and in 2016–2025, 28 of 1,875 names shift from predominantly male to predominantly female use, against two in the reverse direction. These results provide preliminary answers to the research questions and motivate clustering and predictive analysis. They describe aggregate records, not individual identities or causal effects.

1 Introduction

1.1 Goals and research questions

We study how naming preferences change across generations and places, and assess the limits of using a name as a demographic proxy. Three questions organise the analysis.

  1. Do names follow identifiable popularity life cycles, and does spelling help explain when they were popular?
  2. Do states have distinctive naming profiles, and have those profiles become more similar over time?
  3. How stable are name–sex associations, and can earlier spelling and popularity information help anticipate later changes?

These questions concern aggregate associations. A name cannot establish an individual’s sex or gender, and the data do not identify why parents chose it.

The third question builds on two studies cited in our proposal. Lieberson, Dumais and Baumann (2000) emphasise asymmetric changes in androgynous names, particularly declining male use as female use increases. Seguin, Julien and Zhang (2021) emphasise the persistence of many androgynous names and the role of changing spelling preferences. These perspectives motivate examining both the stability of name–sex associations and the direction of substantial shifts. Our threshold-based comparison of historically common names addresses related patterns; it is not a direct replication of either study’s population or definition of androgyny.

1.2 Analytical scope

The study uses two complementary geographical levels: national series from 1880 and state series from 1910, both ending in 2025. The national series provide an aggregate reference, while the state series allow us to examine geographical differences. Comparisons between the datasets use their shared 1910–2025 period and matching recorded-sex categories.

This update presents preparation and exploratory evidence for each question. National data support the analysis of life cycles, spelling and name–sex associations; state data support geographical comparisons. Predictive models remain a subsequent step: descriptive patterns alone do not demonstrate out-of-sample predictive performance.

2 Data

2.1 Sources and observation unit

The data are drawn from the US Social Security Administration’s national and state baby-name datasets. The national data comprise 146 annual yobYYYY.txt files for 1880–2025. Each row gives a name × recorded sex × birth year count, with the year obtained from the filename. The state data comprise 51 files for the 50 states and DC over 1910–2025; each observation additionally identifies the state of birth.

Rows are aggregate counts, not individual births or independent survey responses. National and state observations describe overlapping populations at different geographical levels, so they are analysed in distinct tables.

SSA derives its name statistics from Social Security card applications. Historical coverage is incomplete, particularly before 1937. The agency also notes possible recording errors and treats different spellings separately. Consequently, these data should not be described as a complete birth census. See the SSA background and qualifications.

The national documentation describes records as of 1 March 2026. Exact release alignment between the national and state datasets has not been established; comparisons of their published totals are therefore interpreted descriptively.

Variable Meaning Type
state State abbreviation, including DC; state table only Categorical
sex Recorded F or M category Categorical
year Birth year; derived from filename for national data Integer, temporal
name Published first-name spelling Text
count Published count for that combination Positive integer

2.2 Data wrangling and preprocessing

Both datasets follow the same preparation procedure:

  1. Read the source files with explicit column types, preserving published name strings and checking blank values separately. Extract the national birth year from each filename.
  2. Inspect missing values, duplicate records, recorded-sex categories, years and counts to identify potential data issues.
  3. Derive decade, name length, published popularity share and rank. Compute national measures within sex–year groups and state measures within state–sex–year groups.
  4. Save the prepared national and state tables for analysis.

Preparation retains all 2,181,032 national records and 6,696,687 state records. Inspection found no missing fields or duplicate keys. The data contain 292 national sex–year groups and 11,832 state–sex–year groups. Placeholder-like labels occur in 655 national records and 1,811 state records. These observations are retained because a label alone does not establish a recording error. No rows are removed or imputed.

The four derived features have explicit analytical roles:

Derived field Transformation Purpose
decade Round birth year down to the decade Compare historical periods
name_length Number of characters in the published spelling Describe spelling patterns
published_share Count ÷ total published count in the relevant geography–sex–year group Compare relative popularity across different-sized groups
rank Descending count within the group; alphabetical tie-break Identify leading names and top-ten concentration

The prepared national and state tables contain eight and nine columns, respectively. They combine numerical measures (count, name_length, published_share, rank), categorical fields (sex and, for state data, state), temporal fields (year, decade) and text (name). Derived variables serve the research questions without adding independent source information; the number of aggregate records alone does not establish statistical significance.

The EDA aggregates national records into name trajectories and spelling profiles, and state records into geographical distributions. Female and male counts are pivoted by name and year. Under the publication-threshold assumption, an absent count is represented by a 0–4 interval rather than an observed zero. Analysis-specific filters are stated with each result; placeholder labels are excluded from distinctive-name rankings only.

The published counts sum to 375,362,447 nationally and 330,978,761 across states over their respective periods. For the shared 1910–2025 period, pooled-state totals range from 80.8% to 96.4% of national totals within sex–year groups. These ratios describe the published datasets, not the fraction of births covered.

2.3 Challenges and interpretation rules

The SSA suppresses rare entries for privacy, so an absent record cannot be assumed to represent zero births. Suppression also means that adding state counts does not necessarily reproduce a national count. SSA publication limits and data qualifications describe these restrictions.

Popularity shares use published counts within the stated geography, year and recorded-sex group as their denominator. They are not shares of all births. Female share instead compares F with F + M for the same name and time window. Where an opposite-sex record is absent, we do not automatically assign a female share of 0 or 1. The eligibility rules for each name–sex comparison are stated alongside its results.

3 Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

3.1 Summary statistics and concentration

Year Sex Published counts Distinct names Median top-10 share
1950 F 1,610,017 2,112 28.0%
1950 M 1,720,112 1,721 36.3%
1980 F 1,462,212 3,685 22.2%
1980 M 1,668,069 2,502 27.2%
2025 F 1,303,470 5,349 9.6%
2025 M 1,466,284 4,368 10.5%

Counts sum published state records; distinct names are the union of spellings within each year and sex. The top-ten statistic gives each state/DC equal weight.

The ten leading names account for a substantially smaller share of published counts in 2025 than in 1950: 9.6% versus 28.0% for female records, and 10.5% versus 36.3% for male records in the median state. Female concentration has a local low in 1964 within the 1950–1970 interval. Since 2003, the female and male medians have remained within one percentage point of each other.

This supports diversification among published names. It does not, by itself, show whether states prefer the same names or whether name–sex associations have changed. The following comparisons address those questions directly.

3.2 RQ1: popularity life cycles and spelling

Popular names show narrower periods of high popularity in later peak cohorts. We select 815 national name–sex series whose highest published share occurs between 1900 and 2005 and reaches at least 0.1% of the relevant sex–year total. Each trajectory is divided by its own peak share and aligned on the peak year. Curves use a common window of 20 years before and after the peak, so each cohort contains the same names throughout. The alignment places each maximum at the centre by construction; it does not establish that every name follows a single rise-and-fall cycle.

The median number of observed years at or above half of peak share is 44.5 for names peaking in the 1900s and 45 for those peaking in the 1910s. The corresponding decade medians range from 17 to 23 for peaks from 1950 to 2005 (Figure 2). The measure counts all qualifying years, including any separate periods of renewed popularity; it is not necessarily the length of one continuous rise-and-fall cycle.

The observed pattern is consistent with faster turnover among these selected popular names. Observation boundaries shorten some durations: early names may already have been popular before 1880, and recent names may remain popular after 2025. The bars count qualifying years over the full 1880–2025 record, so their observation periods differ even though the plotted curves share a common window. Consequently, this comparison does not establish that every name’s life cycle has halved or that today’s newly popular names will follow the same path.

Spelling is associated with popularity period. Pooling published counts within each decade, the male share assigned to names ending in “n” rises from 13% in the 1940s to 34% in the 2000s, while “d” endings fall from 16% to 3%. For female counts, “a” endings rise from 31% to 39% and “h” endings from 4% to 7%; “e” endings decline (Figure 3).

These changes make spelling a plausible predictor of a name’s aggregate popularity period. They do not measure how accurately spelling predicts that period for unseen names. The association motivates character-based regression, while the trajectory shapes motivate clustering.

3.3 RQ2: state naming profiles and convergence

The state distributions become more similar under a descriptive comparison. Every five years, we calculate Jensen–Shannon divergence between each state’s name distribution and the pooled other states, separately by recorded sex. The comparison uses names published in both distributions, renormalised to sum to one. Lower divergence means more similar relative frequencies on that shared set of names.

We benchmark each comparison against 30 simulated draws from the pooled other-state distribution, using the focal state’s published total as the draw size and suppressing simulated counts below five. Draws without any published shared name have undefined divergence and are excluded. Subtracting the mean simulated divergence gives a baseline-adjusted measure (Figure 4). This is a descriptive benchmark, not a complete correction: the reference is itself suppressed, observed and simulated shared vocabularies can differ, and published totals are smaller than the underlying populations.

The median across state–sex groups falls from approximately 0.062 bits in 1930 to 0.025 in 1985, a reduction of about 60%, and is about 0.029 in 2025. This is consistent with convergence in the published naming profiles during the middle of the twentieth century. Starting in 1940 instead gives a decline from 0.057 to 0.025 bits by 1985 (56%). Incomplete coverage before 1937 and changing publication support limit the historical comparison; the benchmark does not establish that residual differences are independent of state size.

States also differ in which names are over-represented. For 2016–2025, we divide each name’s share in a state by its share in the pooled other states, within recorded-sex categories. Candidates must have at least 200 published counts in the focal state and a positive count elsewhere. Placeholder labels are excluded from this ranking and its denominators. The selected names have a median ratio of about 4.3 (Figure 5).

Examples include Abdullahi in Minnesota, Rochel and Binyomin in New Jersey, Kai and Kaia in Hawaii, and Landry and Beaux in Louisiana. These are local relative preferences, not necessarily the state’s most common names. Linguistic traditions, community composition and regional culture are possible explanations, but the data contain no ethnicity, religion or parental-motive variables with which to establish them. Suppression and the fixed minimum count also affect rankings, particularly in small states.

3.4 RQ3: stability of name–sex associations

Most eligible names retain a strong association with one recorded-sex category; large endpoint shifts are more often toward female use. We compare each name’s first complete calendar decade with at least 1,000 published counts, occurring no later than the 1990s, with 2016–2025. Names must also reach 1,000 published counts in the recent window. This selects historically common names that remain common, rather than all names ever recorded.

For each period, missing annual sex-specific counts are bounded at 0–4 before calculating lower and upper female shares. A shift qualifies only if the whole interval moves from below 30% to above 70%, or the reverse. This avoids classifying a suppressed opposite-sex count as an observed zero.

Among 1,875 eligible names, 1,723 (91.9%) remain predominantly associated with the same category at both endpoints. Twenty-eight shift from predominantly male to predominantly female use and two shift in the reverse direction. This directional imbalance is evidence about this selected cohort, not a universal rule or an estimated probability that any new name will switch. Names that declined below the recent threshold are excluded, so the comparison cannot establish the prevalence of switching among all historical names.

The share of published counts assigned to names with female shares between 20% and 80% lies between 1.8% and 4.3% in 1985, versus 5.8%–9.9% in 2025. The lower limit counts names whose full female-share interval is inside the 20%–80% range; the upper limit also counts names whose interval overlaps it. Rare names widen these bounds, but the 2025 lower limit still exceeds the 1985 upper limit. Shared name use has therefore increased under this definition even after allowing for threshold suppression. This describes aggregate usage, not an individual’s identity.

Selection ranks names by total published counts over 1880–2025. Trajectories show only years with at least 200 published counts; lines are interval midpoints and shading shows the suppression bounds.

The selected male-to-female examples are Kelly, Taylor, Leslie, Morgan, Riley and Avery; the reverse examples are Elisha and Santana. Their trajectories show that endpoint changes can conceal reversals or periods of mixed use. A shift need not be permanent or follow one common timetable. Their shapes motivate using past popularity and share changes as predictors; prospective performance still requires evaluation on later periods.

4 Analysis

4.1 Preliminary findings and interpretation

The completed analysis gives a first answer to each question. For RQ1, later peak cohorts spend fewer observed years near peak popularity, and spelling patterns change across eras. For RQ2, shared-name distributions become more similar over much of the twentieth century while retaining local relative preferences. For RQ3, the selected common-name cohort shows a marked directional imbalance in large association shifts.

These findings are descriptive. Peak-based selection, continued-popularity requirements, suppression and changing historical coverage all affect which names can be compared. The state benchmark is conditional on published data; it does not isolate cultural effects. None of the analyses establishes individual characteristics from a name or the causes of parental choices.

4.2 Proposed methods and validation

The following methods are planned; no clustering or predictive model has yet been fitted.

  • Popularity trajectories: k-means clustering. Represent each national name–sex series by an equal-length vector of annual published popularity shares over a common observation window, normalised by its maximum share. Apply k-means, which minimises within-cluster squared Euclidean distances, to identify recurring trajectory shapes. Compare candidate numbers of clusters using silhouette scores, repeated initialisations and stability across periods and minimum-count rules. Truncated trajectories and suppressed counts require explicit treatment; absent records will not automatically be interpreted as zero.
  • Spelling and popularity period: ridge regression. Use character n-grams to predict the count-weighted mean birth year of each name–sex series. Ridge regression applies an L2 penalty to limit overfitting with many correlated spelling features. Select the penalty through cross-validation within the training set and evaluate held-out mean absolute error, in years, against training-mean and final-letter baselines. Keep all observations with the same spelling in one partition. The target describes an aggregate popularity period, not an individual’s age.
  • State profiles: hierarchical clustering. Within each decade and recorded-sex category, construct state naming distributions on one common vocabulary. Apply average-linkage hierarchical clustering to pairwise Jensen–Shannon distances, the square root of Jensen–Shannon divergence. Assess whether state groupings persist across decades and alternative vocabulary and suppression treatments. Divergence from a pooled reference alone cannot supply the required pairwise distance matrix.
  • Name–sex shifts: logistic regression. Define a binary outcome for a transition from below 30% to above 70% female share, or the reverse, between fixed historical and subsequent windows. Use L2-penalised logistic regression with a small set of earlier spelling, popularity and female-share features. Eligibility will use information available at the prediction date; suppression-ambiguous future outcomes will be reported separately. Evaluate on later periods using precision–recall curves, average precision and counts of observed and correctly identified shifts, alongside no-shift and training-prevalence baselines.

For prediction, feature extraction, preprocessing and penalty selection will use training data only. Name-grouped splits test generalisation to unseen spellings; chronological splits test prediction of future changes. Training outcome windows must end before the evaluation period. Period, count and share thresholds will be varied to assess sensitivity to these definitions. The 28 male-to-female and two reverse endpoint shifts in the EDA do not establish sufficient events for prospective modelling. If fixed-window samples contain too few shifts for meaningful training and evaluation, this part will remain descriptive.

5 Conclusion and Next Steps

Data preparation and exploratory analysis are complete for the national and state datasets. The descriptive results address all three research questions: later peak cohorts have shorter observed high-popularity periods, state profiles become more similar under the chosen divergence measure, and large name–sex shifts are more frequent toward female use in the selected cohort. These findings remain subject to suppression, historical coverage and sample-selection limitations. The proposed models have not yet been fitted.

The next steps are:

  1. Prepare modelling datasets. Define common trajectory windows, character n-gram features and state–decade profiles; fix prediction windows, eligibility rules and training/test partitions before fitting.
  2. Fit and evaluate the proposed models. Apply k-means, ridge regression and hierarchical clustering as specified in Section 4.2. Fit logistic regression only if fixed-window samples contain enough shifts for meaningful training and evaluation. Compare predictive performance with the stated baselines on held-out names or later periods, as appropriate.
  3. Check robustness and complete the final report. Vary observation windows, count/share thresholds and vocabulary choices; assess cluster stability and identify which conclusions persist. Integrate the results, limitations and reproducible code into the final Quarto report.

Reproducibility

Run notebooks/01_state_preparation.ipynb, then notebooks/02_state_eda.ipynb with Python 3.12 and the dependencies in requirements.txt. The EDA notebook contains the methods, code and results; it saves seven figures in reports/figures/ and numerical outputs in reports/tables/. Simulations use seed 2026. Render with quarto render reports/update_AJ.qmd; the HTML embeds its figures.
